---
title: The precision-recall curve, for a rare class
version: 1
---

The ROC curve plots recall against the false positive rate. The **precision-recall curve** plots
precision against recall, across the same cuts, and on a rare class it tells a different and more
honest story:

```schooling-figure

```

**The curve starts high and falls fast.** The handful of subscribers the model is surest about are
leavers more than half the time; reach for more of the leavers and precision drops towards the 6.1%
of leavers among all test rows, which is the dotted line and the precision of sending everybody a
credit.

**That dotted line is the baseline, and it moves with the data.** On the ROC chart the knows-nothing
model is always the diagonal; on this one it sits at the share of positives, here 0.061. A model on a
problem with 1% positives and one with 30% cannot be compared by eye on this chart, and that is a
feature: it keeps the rarity of the class in front of the reader.

The dashed line at 0.278 is the precision where a credit pays for itself. **Wherever the curve is above it,
the credits sent at that cut make money on average**; where it drops below, they lose it. That is the
picture of lesson 1's economics, and it is a picture the ROC curve cannot draw.

## Average precision

The area under this curve, computed as **average precision**, was the second number in `ranking.py`:
**0.322**, against 0.061 for a model that knows nothing, so about five times the baseline. It reads as
the precision averaged over every recall level, and like AUC it needs no cut.

**On a rare class, prefer average precision to AUC for comparing models**, because it is driven by the
top of the ranking, where the decisions are made. The ROC AUC of 0.804 sounds like a strong model;
the average precision of 0.322 says, more truthfully, that most of the subscribers it is suspicious of
stay anyway. Report both, and know which question each one answers.
